text:
I need help with the narrative section of a grant application. I'm the director of a volunteer-run food bank in a town of about 9,000 people, and we're applying to our county community foundation for a refrigerated van.

What I have:
- We hand out about 38,000 pounds of food a month to 610 households. About 6,000 pounds of that is fresh produce, milk and eggs.
- Last summer, local farms offered us roughly 9,000 pounds of produce over three months that we had to turn down because we had no way to pick it up cold or store it.
- The van costs $68,000. We're asking the foundation for $50,000 and covering the other $18,000 from our reserves, which would leave us with $11,000.
- We have 23 regular volunteers. Four of them have said they would drive the van on a weekly schedule.
- The foundation gave us $12,000 for shelving in 2023. Our final report on that grant was four months late.

I want the narrative to say the van will let us double the amount of fresh food we hand out in the first year. The narrative is limited to 500 words.

Before I draft, there's one problem with the numbers and a few gaps I'd like to fill.

**The doubling claim doesn't fit your own figures.** You hand out 6,000 lb of fresh food a month, which is about 72,000 lb a year. Doubling it means finding another 72,000 lb. The only evidence you've given me is the 9,000 lb you turned down last summer. That's about 12% more for the year, not 100%. A foundation reviewer can work that out in a minute, and an overclaim is worse than a smaller, solid number. That's especially true with a funder that will compare your next report against this one. So I'd like to know whether you have anything that supports a bigger figure.

1. **Are there more sources the van would open up?** For example, grocery store rescue, a regional food bank's fresh allocation you can't collect now, farms outside summer, or farms that haven't offered because they know you can't take it. Anything you can put a number on, even a rough one, helps. If not, I'd suggest a goal like "recover at least 9,000 lb of fresh food a year that we now turn away."
2. **Where would the extra food be kept cold?** You said you couldn't pick it up cold *or store it*. A van solves the pickup. Do you have enough cooler space, or would you distribute the same day?
3. **How will you pay to run the van?** I mean insurance, fuel, maintenance and registration. Do you have a rough annual cost and where the money comes from? With only $11,000 left in reserves, a reviewer will ask.
4. **What caused the late report on the 2023 shelving grant, and what's changed since?** For example, a new volunteer who handles reporting, or a calendar system. The foundation will remember the late report. A short line owning it and saying what's fixed will go over better than leaving it out. Did the shelving produce results you can mention?
5. **Do the farms or the four drivers have anything in writing?** A letter of support from a farm or a signed driver schedule would strengthen the case. Also, do you track how many households get fresh food or ask for it?

If you don't know some of these, that's fine. I'll write without them rather than guess.

You're right, the numbers don't support doubling. Go with your suggestion, recovering at least 9,000 lb a year that we now turn away. I can't promise the farms will offer the same 9,000 again, though.

1. I don't know of other sources I can put a number on.
2. I don't know.
3. Insurance and fuel come to about $4,500 a year. It's not in our budget yet.
4. Our treasurer at the time was in the hospital for most of that period. Our treasurer now is Dave Lin. I can commit to naming Dave as responsible for the final report, due 30 days after the grant year ends. I can also commit to sending the foundation our fresh food pounds every quarter. I don't know about results from the shelving.
5. Two of the farms have written letters saying they'll give again if we can pick up cold. Nothing in writing from the drivers that I know of. I don't know about tracking households for fresh food.

I've written it at about 430 words, so you have room to add a line or two.

<final_document>
**Project Narrative: Refrigerated Van for Fresh Food Recovery**

[Food Bank Name] is a volunteer-run food bank serving [Town], a community of about 9,000 people. Each month, our 23 regular volunteers hand out about 38,000 pounds of food to 610 households. About 6,000 pounds of that is fresh produce, milk and eggs. Families struggle most to afford these foods, and they are also the hardest for us to get.

**The problem**

Last summer, local farms offered us roughly 9,000 pounds of fresh produce over three months. We had to turn it all down. We had no way to pick it up cold, so it would have spoiled before it reached anyone. That is about six weeks of our current fresh food supply, lost because we didn't have the right vehicle.

**Our request**

We are asking the foundation for $50,000 toward a $68,000 refrigerated van. We will cover the remaining $18,000 from our own reserves. That is more than a quarter of the cost, and a serious commitment for an organization our size.

**What the van will do**

The van will let us collect fresh food from farms and keep it cold on the way to our distribution. Two of the farms that offered produce last summer have written letters, attached, saying they will give again if we can pick up cold. Four of our volunteers have said they will drive the van on a weekly schedule.

Our goal for the first year is to recover at least 9,000 pounds of fresh food that we would otherwise have to turn away. That is the amount farms offered us last summer. Harvests vary and farms make their own decisions, so we can't guarantee the same amount again. We will report what we actually receive. At that level, the van would increase the fresh food we hand out by about one-eighth, with all of it going to families already on our rolls.

We estimate that insurance and fuel for the van will cost about $4,500 a year.

**Accountability**

Our final report on the foundation's 2023 shelving grant was four months late. Our treasurer at the time was in the hospital for most of that period. We regret the delay. Our current treasurer, Dave Lin, will be responsible for this grant's final report, due 30 days after the grant year ends. We will also send the foundation our fresh food totals every quarter, so you can follow the results through the year.

**Why now**

The food is there, and local farms want to give it. A refrigerated van is the one thing standing between that food and the 610 households we serve.
</final_document>

Before you send it:

- **Fill in the placeholders:** [Food Bank Name] and [Town].
- **Say how the $4,500 a year will be paid.** I gave the cost but not where the money comes from, because you don't know yet. Reviewers will notice that this cost isn't covered and that your reserves will be down to $11,000. One sentence would close that gap, for example "we will add this to our 2027 operating budget" or "a local business has agreed to cover insurance." Only use it if it's true.
- **Check your cold storage.** The draft doesn't claim you can store extra fresh food, since you weren't sure. If you can't, someone may ask where 9,000 lb of produce goes after pickup. If the answer is that you hand it out the same day or within a day or two, it's worth adding.
- **Confirm the drivers.** Before you submit, it would help to have the four drivers confirm in writing, even by email.
- **Attach the two farm letters.** The draft says they're attached.
